name: 5:2 diet
lead: The 5:2 diet, also called the Fast Diet, is an intermittent fasting pattern in which people eat normally for five days a week and limit intake to roughly 500 to 600 calories on two non-consecutive days, about a quarter of usual energy intake.[1] It was popularised in the UK and Australia by the doctor and broadcaster Michael Mosley after a 2012 BBC Horizon documentary, and a 2013 book co-written with Mimi Spencer turned it into a mass-market diet brand.[1][21]

People use it to lose body fat and become leaner, which changes how the face and body look: less facial and abdominal fat, a more visible jawline and cheekbones, and a lower body-fat percentage. Because the restriction is confined to two days, followers often describe it as easier to sustain than eating a little less every day, and it is used as a way to create a weekly calorie deficit without tracking food on the other five days.[1][5] Lifters and physique-focused dieters also discuss it as a way to trim fat while keeping most days at normal intake.

Randomized trials have compared it with continuous calorie restriction and other diets in people with obesity, type 2 diabetes and fatty liver disease.[2][3][4][11][12] Reviews and meta-analyses generally report weight loss similar to other calorie-restriction approaches, with improvements in several metabolic markers; long-term outcomes are less well studied.[1][5][7][13]

angle.text: The 5:2 diet is used as a structured way to cut calories and lose fat. As body fat falls, facial contours, jaw definition and waist-to-hip proportions change, which is the appearance payoff followers describe. Trials report average weight loss comparable to ordinary calorie restriction.

paras: The 5:2 diet is one of the main forms of intermittent fasting, alongside alternate-day fasting, time-restricted eating and periodic whole-day fasting.[1][6][23] In alternate-day fasting a fast day of under 25 percent of usual energy needs alternates with a non-fasting day, while time-restricted eating confines food to a daily window of about 8 to 12 hours; 5:2 sits between them as a weekly pattern.[23] On the two restricted days, which are usually not consecutive, people eat roughly 500 to 600 calories, around 25 percent of regular intake; on the other five days they eat without a prescribed limit.[1] The original trials focused on calorie content rather than a particular food pattern.[22]

Trial versions have used a fixed formula diet or ordinary food on fast days.[8][11] Published popular versions typically suggest spreading the fast-day calories across one or two small meals rich in protein and vegetables, and following the two fast days with ordinary eating, although exact menus vary by book and programme.[21]

Supporters describe it as a flexible alternative to daily dieting: social meals and training days can be arranged around the schedule. Researchers examining fasting regimens note that many people find short fasts tolerable in trials of up to three months, with compliance above 80 percent in the shorter trials in one meta-analysis.[7]

Fasting is practised across many cultures and religions, and therapeutic fasts for obesity have been investigated since at least 1915. Medical interest revived in the 1960s after an enthusiastic report from Bloom and colleagues, when early regimens lasted from one to 14 days.[1][23]

The 5:2 pattern was first documented in a 2011 article co-authored by Michelle Harvie, Mark Mattson and colleagues.[1][22] Mattson, an American neuroscientist who headed the Laboratory of Neurosciences at the US National Institute on Aging and later wrote The Intermittent Fasting Revolution (MIT Press, 2022), studies intermittent fasting and the brain.[22] Harvie's group in Manchester ran trials of intermittent restriction in overweight women.[1]

Michael Mosley (born 1957, died 5 June 2024) trained as a doctor, joined the BBC in 1985 and became a prominent science presenter.[21] He learned of the approach from Mattson and presented it in the 2012 BBC2 Horizon documentary Eat, Fast and Live Longer, in which Mattson also appeared.[1][21][22] The Fast Diet, written with Mimi Spencer, was published by Short Books in early 2013.[21] Mosley later promoted other plans, including The Clever Gut Diet (2017) and The Fast 800 (2019), a low-carbohydrate Mediterranean-style plan with an 800-calorie daily target, and hosted the BBC Radio 4 series Just One Thing from 2021.[21]

Books, meal packages, coaching and supplements were subsequently marketed around the regimen.[1] A 2018 survey by the International Food Information Council named intermittent fasting the most popular diet among respondents, and the pattern became fashionable in Silicon Valley circles.[1][23] Critics quoted in a Wikipedia summary have described some of the commercial coaching and meal products as expensive and not backed by science.[23]

Mosley's death while hiking on the Greek island of Symi in June 2024 brought a wave of retrospective coverage of his diet work; an inquest in December 2024 recorded the cause of death as unascertainable, most likely heat stroke or an unidentified pathological cause.[21] In his final interview he acknowledged finding many of his own health tips hard to follow.[21]

Online, the 5:2 diet is discussed in diet, fitness and physique forums as one option among intermittent fasting schedules. A 2021 report of the PLoS One randomized trial was shared on Hacker News under a headline stating that the diet did not significantly increase long-term weight loss.[19][20]

Most human studies of intermittent fasting report weight loss of about 2.5 to 9.9 percent of body weight, mostly fat mass with some lean mass, and limited evidence of an advantage over continuous calorie restriction.[1][23] A review of cardiometabolic outcomes found that alternate-day fasting, the 5:2 diet and time-restricted eating all produced mild to moderate weight loss (1 to 8 percent from baseline) and 10 to 30 percent reductions in energy intake, with decreases in blood pressure, insulin resistance and oxidative stress, and variable effects on LDL cholesterol and triglycerides.[6]

A 2023 network meta-analysis of 24 randomized trials (1,768 participants) found that intermittent fasting regimens produced weight loss similar to continuous energy restriction (mean difference 0.26 kg, not statistically significant), ranking alternate-day fasting first, followed by continuous restriction and time-restricted eating.[7] An umbrella review of 11 meta-analyses covering 130 randomized trials, with a median follow-up of three months, graded the quality of evidence for many obesity-related outcomes.[5] A 2024 umbrella review and network meta-analysis of ten meta-analyses (153 original studies, 9,846 participants) compared time-restricted eating, alternate-day fasting and the 5:2 diet with continuous restriction on metabolic outcomes.[14] A 2024 meta-analysis compared intermittent and continuous energy restriction for body composition and cardiometabolic markers.[15] A 2015 review in the International Journal of Obesity examined whether fasting is a passing fad or an effective strategy for weight loss and weight maintenance.[13]

A review in Nature Reviews Endocrinology noted that intermittent fasting diets can produce clinically significant weight loss while few studies had examined health benefits in humans at the time.[2] Wikipedia notes that fasting does not appear to improve athletic performance, and that fasted exercise lasting longer than 60 minutes can reduce performance.[1][23]

Modified alternate-day fasting, time-restricted eating (such as a 16:8 eating window), periodic multi-day fasts and the 800-calorie Fast 800 plan are related approaches that appear in the same literature and popular books.[21][23] Some people pair fast days with resistance training or high-intensity intervals; one randomized trial tested a 5:2 formula-diet arm against a 5:2 exercise arm in adults with type 2 diabetes.[11] Physique-oriented dieters sometimes use fast days with the aim of preserving training quality on the other days, while the review literature notes that fasted exercise beyond about an hour can reduce performance.[23]

Reported early effects include constant hunger, irritability, dizziness, nausea, headaches and impaired thinking, usually fading within about a month.[1] Dropout rates in one 2019 review ranged from 2 to 38 percent for intermittent fasting versus 0 to 50 percent for calorie restriction.[23] The cardiometabolic review concluded that intermittent fasting did not increase disordered-eating behaviours or disturb energy levels in the trials examined.[6]

The diet is not recommended for pregnant or breastfeeding women, children and adolescents, older adults, underweight people, and people with or at risk of eating disorders.[1][23] The US National Institute on Aging describes the research as limited and does not recommend it for the general public; the American Heart Association has said good evidence of heart benefits is lacking, and the UK NHS advises people to consult a physician first.[1][23]

Mosley's related Channel 4 programme Lose a Stone in 21 Days, which proposed 800 calories a day, drew criticism from some medical experts, and the eating-disorder charity Beat reported 51 percent more contacts to its helpline during the broadcast period.[21]

A 50-week randomized trial tested intermittent calorie restriction in the form of the 5:2 diet against continuous calorie restriction for body weight, body composition, adipose tissue gene expression and metabolism.[3]

A pilot randomized study in 24 obese male war veterans compared two non-consecutive days of about 600 calories plus five ad libitum days with a standard energy-restricted diet over six weeks, asking whether 5:2 could achieve at least 5 percent weight loss.[8]

A 12-week randomized trial in 74 people with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease compared the 5:2 diet and a low-carbohydrate high-fat diet with a control group on liver fat.[4] A 12-week randomized trial in 60 adults with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and abnormal glucose compared intermittent and continuous calorie restriction, and a further randomized trial studied intermittent restriction in non-diabetic patients with that condition.[16][17] A 2023 meta-analysis examined intermittent fasting on hepatic end points in fatty liver disease.[10]

A three-arm randomized trial in adults with overweight or obesity and type 2 diabetes compared a 5:2 diet (formula diet two days a week) and a 5:2 exercise programme of high-intensity interval and resistance training with routine lifestyle education, measuring glycemic control and cardiometabolic health.[11] Controlled trials in subjects with and without type 2 diabetes have also reported 5:2 effects on insulin secretion and sensitivity and on cardiovascular risk factors.[12][18]

A separate randomised controlled trial of the 5:2 diet published in PLoS One in 2021 was reported on Hacker News under a headline stating that it did not significantly increase long-term weight loss.[19][20] A randomized trial also examined whether metabolic improvements under calorie restriction depended on gut microbiome composition.[9]

lore.intro: In diet and fitness communities the 5:2 diet is discussed as a lower-effort alternative to daily calorie counting, alongside 16:8 and alternate-day schedules; claims below come from the diet's popular presentation and trial literature.[1][20]

claims.claim: Two low-calorie days a week make fat loss easier to stick with than daily dieting
claims.believers: Followers and authors of the popular books say that confining restriction to two days feels more manageable and leaves five days of normal social eating.[21]
claims.experts: Trials report weight loss similar to continuous restriction, and one meta-analysis found compliance above 80 percent in trials shorter than three months; dropout ranged from 2 to 38 percent in one review.[7][23]

claims.claim: 5:2 produces more fat loss than eating the same calories continuously
claims.believers: Early enthusiasm held that periodic fasting might have special metabolic effects beyond the calories saved.[2]
claims.experts: A 2023 meta-analysis found intermittent regimens comparable to continuous restriction (mean difference 0.26 kg), and the 50-week trial compared the two directly.[3][7]

claims.claim: Fast days improve insulin sensitivity and metabolic health
claims.believers: Advocates cite lower insulin and improved markers on fast days.[6]
claims.experts: Reviews report improvements in insulin resistance and blood pressure with variable effects on LDL and triglycerides; trials in type 2 diabetes have measured insulin secretion and sensitivity.[6][12]

claims.claim: Fasting protects muscle and works well alongside training
claims.believers: Some lifters say they keep strength on normal days while cutting fat.[11]
claims.experts: Studies report loss of mostly fat mass with some lean mass, and reviews note fasted exercise longer than 60 minutes can reduce performance.[1][23]

claims.claim: The diet is safe for anyone
claims.believers: Popular accounts present it as flexible and widely suitable.[21]
claims.experts: It is not recommended for pregnancy, adolescents, older adults, underweight people or people with eating disorders, and the NIA does not recommend it for the general public.[1][23]

claims.claim: The 5:2 diet leads to lasting long-term weight loss
claims.believers: Book and programme marketing presents it as a long-term lifestyle.[1][21]
claims.experts: The 2021 PLoS One randomised trial was reported as not significantly increasing long-term weight loss, and reviews note long-term data are limited.[19][20][23]

card.summary: Eat normally five days, eat about 500 calories on two; weight loss is similar to ordinary dieting.
card.note: Not advised for pregnancy, adolescents, or people with eating-disorder histories.

quick.overview:
The 5:2 diet has people eat normally five days a week and eat very little on two non-consecutive days. It was popularised in 2012.

Trials and meta-analyses report weight loss comparable to continuous calorie restriction.
quick.mechanism: The two low-calorie days create a weekly energy deficit; researchers also examine effects on insulin, liver fat and adipose tissue.
quick.risks: Hunger, irritability and headaches are reported early. It is not recommended for pregnancy, youth, older adults, underweight people or those with eating disorders.
